prompt: Put the lesson's questions before writing a plugin in order.
items: does the web already do it?
write one, as small as the job allows

prompt: What is the cost the lesson names for a plugin of your own?

choices.text: A licence fee to Capacitor
Apps that run slower than with the official plugins
Native code you maintain on two platforms, for years
choices.why: Right, through every Capacitor and system release.

choices.text: A review of each release by Capacitor's own team

prompt: A community plugin does what you need, and its last release targets Capacitor 5. What does the lesson warn?

choices.text: It holds your whole app back on an old Capacitor
choices.why: Right. Read the last release date before installing one.

choices.text: Community plugins cannot be used in a store app
Old plugins run faster, having had longer to be tuned
Nothing; versions do not matter for plugins

prompt: A team's web feature works in Chrome on a laptop and they ship it in the Capacitor app without a plugin. What should they have checked, by the lesson?

choices.text: That Chrome is up to date
choices.why: Chrome on a laptop is not what runs the app.

choices.text: That the feature has a TypeScript type
choices.why: Types do not say a WebView supports it.

choices.text: That the store allows web APIs
That both systems' WebViews support it
choices.why: Right. A WebView is not the browser it is built from.

prompt: What joins the TypeScript side of a plugin to its Kotlin and Swift sides?

choices.text: The version in package.json, compared across the three sides
choices.why: Versions do not join the sides.

choices.text: The same name, and the same method names
A generated file that sync checks
choices.why: Nothing checks it before the app runs.

choices.text: The folder each side is in, as package.json names it
choices.why: Folders tell cap where the code is, not what it answers.

prompt: Match each folder of the generated plugin to what it holds.

pairs.right: the interface and the web implementation

prompt: The generated package.json uses ^8.0.0 ranges, while the planner pins exact versions. Why is that right for the plugin?

choices.text: Ranges are faster to install than exact versions
The app pins, not the library
choices.why: Right. A library says what it works with, and the app that installs it holds the lockfile.

choices.text: npm refuses exact versions in plugins
It is wrong, and the lesson pins them

prompt: In src/index.ts, what does the web option of registerPlugin do?

choices.text: It runs on phones as well, as a fallback
choices.why: On a phone, Capacitor finds the native class.

choices.text: It disables the plugin in browsers, so the web build stays small
It publishes the plugin to the web
Loads src/web.ts in a browser, the first time it is needed
choices.why: Right. There is no native class there.

prompt: Why did the lesson remove the generated test target from Package.swift?

choices.text: It named a deleted test
choices.why: Right: it pointed at the deleted iOS test, which tested echo.

choices.text: Swift Package Manager rejects tests
Plugins must not have tests
choices.why: The lesson says a real plugin deserves them.

choices.text: To make the build faster

prompt: Why does the interface carry isSupported()?

choices.text: Capacitor requires it in every plugin, or sync refuses it
To tell iOS which version is installed
To ask before offering a button
choices.why: Right. The app asks first, because not every platform keeps the screen on.

choices.text: To ask the person for permission
choices.why: Keeping the screen on needs none on a phone.

prompt: Where did the plugin's README text for keepAwake() come from?

choices.text: A comment in definitions.ts
choices.why: Right. npm run build runs docgen over the interface.

choices.text: Written by hand in README.md
Capacitor's website, copied in by the generator
The Kotlin annotation

prompt: What does this.unavailable(…) give the planner that a plain thrown Error would not?

choices.text: A retry, done by the bridge
A dialog shown to the person
The code UNAVAILABLE, told apart from a refusal
A message translated into the person's language

prompt: On the web, the plugin keeps the screen on with navigator.___.request("screen").
A Kotlin plugin method neither resolves nor rejects its call. What does the planner see?

choices.text: An error after thirty seconds
It stays pending
choices.why: Right: a Promise that never settles, the classic bug of a first plugin.

choices.text: undefined, at once
The app closes

prompt: Match each line to what it does.

pairs.right: keeps an Android window's screen on
stops iOS dimming and locking the screen
moves the change to Android's main thread
moves the change to iOS's main thread

prompt: The Swift class adds a method keepAwakeFor but leaves pluginMethods as it was. What happens when the planner calls it?

choices.text: It works on iOS, since the method exists
choices.why: On iOS a method missing from pluginMethods is not reachable.

choices.text: It fails on every platform
choices.why: Only the side missing it fails.

choices.text: Xcode refuses to build
choices.why: It builds; the list is read at run time.

choices.text: The call fails on iOS only
choices.why: Right. Android finds methods by their annotation.

prompt: Why was neither native file compiled for this course?

choices.text: Capacitor forbids compiling a plugin outside the app that uses it
Kotlin cannot be compiled on Linux
No Android SDK and no Xcode on the recording machine
The files were only examples, to be read and never built
choices.why: They are the plugin's real files.

prompt: What does npm install ../keep-awake write into the planner's package.json?

choices.text: "capacitor-keep-awake": "file:../keep-awake"
choices.why: Right. It links the folder rather than copying it.

choices.text: "capacitor-keep-awake": "^0.0.1"
choices.why: A folder install is written as a file: dependency.

choices.text: Nothing; a folder cannot be a dependency, only a registry package
"capacitor-keep-awake": "latest"

prompt: How many Capacitor plugins did cap sync find for Android after the install?
Without --grant screen-wake-lock, what did the status line say?

choices.text: the screen stays on
Nothing at all: the button failed without a word on the screen
This browser cannot keep the screen on.
choices.why: Chromium has the API; it refused.

choices.text: awake failed: Wake Lock permission request denied
choices.why: Right, the browser's words, reported like any failure.

prompt: On a phone, what question does the person answer before the screen stays on?

choices.text: A permission dialog, like the camera's
None
choices.why: Right. Keeping the screen on needs no permission on either system.

choices.text: A notification asking to confirm
The store's question at install

prompt: You rename keepAwake to stayAwake in definitions.ts and web.ts only, and the browser test passes. What breaks, and where?

choices.text: Nothing, since TypeScript checked every call against the interface
choices.why: TypeScript only sees the TypeScript side.

choices.text: The call, on Android and iOS, when it is first made
choices.why: Right. The native sides still answer keepAwake, and nothing checks the names before the app runs.

choices.text: The web build, at the next npm run build
cap sync refuses the plugin, since the names no longer match
choices.why: sync does not read method names.
